question: What dropout rate did the base Transformer use, and at which points in the network was dropout applied?
answer: The base Transformer uses a dropout rate of 0.1 [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 8, Section 5.4 Regularization][Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 8, Section 6.1 Machine Translation]. Dropout is applied to the sums of the token embeddings and positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder stacks [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 8, Section 5.4 Regularization]. It is also applied to the output of each sub‑layer, before that output is added to the sub‑layer input and normalized [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 8, Section 5.4 Regularization].
answer_raw: The base Transformer uses a dropout rate of 0.1 [P1][P3]. Dropout is applied to the sums of the token embeddings and positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder stacks [P1]. It is also applied to the output of each sub‑layer, before that output is added to the sub‑layer input and normalized [P2].

question: Why does scaled dot-product attention divide the dot products by the square root of d_k?
answer: Scaled dot‑product attention divides the dot products by √d_k to prevent the dot products from becoming large in magnitude, which would push the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients; the scaling counteracts this effect [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 4, Section 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention].
answer_raw: Scaled dot‑product attention divides the dot products by √d_k to prevent the dot products from becoming large in magnitude, which would push the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients; the scaling counteracts this effect [P1].

question: Did learned positional embeddings beat sinusoidal positional encodings in the Transformer experiments, and why did the authors keep the sinusoidal version?
answer: Learned positional embeddings did not outperform the sinusoidal positional encodings; the experiments showed nearly identical results for both approaches [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 9, Section 6.2 Model Variations][Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 6, Section 3.5 Positional Encoding]. The authors kept the sinusoidal version because they hypothesized it would let the model attend by relative positions and potentially extrapolate to longer sequences than seen during training [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 6, Section 3.5 Positional Encoding].
answer_raw: Learned positional embeddings did not outperform the sinusoidal positional encodings; the experiments showed nearly identical results for both approaches [P2][P1]. The authors kept the sinusoidal version because they hypothesized it would let the model attend by relative positions and potentially extrapolate to longer sequences than seen during training [P1].

question: What is Inner Monologue in Moshi and what does it improve?
answer: Inner Monologue is a feature of Moshi that jointly models the textual representation of the system’s own speech together with its audio tokens, inserting a text stream as a prefix to the generation of semantic tokens and aligning it to the audio framerate [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, pp. 15-16, Section 3.4.4 Inner Monologue]. It provides a scaffolding that raises the linguistic quality of the generated speech [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, pp. 15-16, Section 3.4.4 Inner Monologue]. In spoken question‑answering benchmarks, Inner Monologue almost triples Moshi’s accuracy and yields the best overall performance while only marginally increasing inference cost [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 29, Section 5.5 Spoken question answering]. It also enables Moshi to model both semantic and acoustic tokens jointly, allowing handling of interactions between arbitrary voices [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 29, Section 5.5 Spoken question answering].
answer_raw: Inner Monologue is a feature of Moshi that jointly models the textual representation of the system’s own speech together with its audio tokens, inserting a text stream as a prefix to the generation of semantic tokens and aligning it to the audio framerate [P3]. It provides a scaffolding that raises the linguistic quality of the generated speech [P3]. In spoken question‑answering benchmarks, Inner Monologue almost triples Moshi’s accuracy and yields the best overall performance while only marginally increasing inference cost [P2]. It also enables Moshi to model both semantic and acoustic tokens jointly, allowing handling of interactions between arbitrary voices [P2].

question: What is Moshi's theoretical latency versus its latency in practice, and what acoustic delay setting gives the theoretical figure?
answer: Moshi achieves a theoretical latency of 160 ms and a practical latency of about 200 ms [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, pp. 1-2, Section Abstract]. This theoretical figure is obtained by pretraining with an acoustic delay of 2 and then fine‑tuning with an acoustic delay of 1 [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 26, Section 5.3 Ablations on generative modeling].
answer_raw: Moshi achieves a theoretical latency of 160 ms and a practical latency of about 200 ms [P3]. This theoretical figure is obtained by pretraining with an acoustic delay of 2 and then fine‑tuning with an acoustic delay of 1 [P1].

question: Which dataset gave Moshi its full-duplex ability, and what property of that dataset made it suitable?
answer: Moshi gains its full‑duplex ability by fine‑tuning on the Fisher dataset (Cieri et al., 2004) [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 8, Section 3.2.2 Pre-training data filtering]. The Fisher dataset consists of two‑speaker conversational recordings, providing naturally occurring turn‑taking and bidirectional speech that makes it suitable for learning full‑duplex dialogue behavior [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 8, Section 3.2.2 Pre-training data filtering].
answer_raw: Moshi gains its full‑duplex ability by fine‑tuning on the Fisher dataset (Cieri et al., 2004) [P2]. The Fisher dataset consists of two‑speaker conversational recordings, providing naturally occurring turn‑taking and bidirectional speech that makes it suitable for learning full‑duplex dialogue behavior [P2].

question: How does H-Net's routing module decide where to place chunk boundaries?
answer: H‑Net’s routing module computes a similarity score between each pair of adjacent encoder outputs using cosine similarity, where a drop in similarity signals a contextual shift [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, arXiv:2507.07955v2, p. 6, Section 2.2.1 Chunking Layer]. It projects the current output \(\hat x_t\) to a query \(q_t\) and the previous output \(\hat x_{t-1}\) to a key \(k_{t-1}\), then forms a boundary probability \(p_t = \tfrac12\bigl(1 - \frac{q_t^{\top}k_{t-1}}{\|q_t\|\|k_{t-1}\|}\bigr)\) which lies in [0,1] [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, arXiv:2507.07955v2, p. 6, Section 2.2.1 Chunking Layer]. A binary boundary indicator \(b_t\) is set to 1 whenever \(p_t \ge 0.5\), otherwise 0, with the first position forced to be a boundary (\(p_1=1.0\)) [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, arXiv:2507.07955v2, p. 6, Section 2.2.1 Chunking Layer].
answer_raw: H‑Net’s routing module computes a similarity score between each pair of adjacent encoder outputs using cosine similarity, where a drop in similarity signals a contextual shift [P3]. It projects the current output \(\hat x_t\) to a query \(q_t\) and the previous output \(\hat x_{t-1}\) to a key \(k_{t-1}\), then forms a boundary probability \(p_t = \tfrac12\bigl(1 - \frac{q_t^{\top}k_{t-1}}{\|q_t\|\|k_{t-1}\|}\bigr)\) which lies in [0,1] [P3]. A binary boundary indicator \(b_t\) is set to 1 whenever \(p_t \ge 0.5\), otherwise 0, with the first position forced to be a boundary (\(p_1=1.0\)) [P3].

question: What problem does H-Net's ratio loss address, and what weight alpha is used for it?
answer: H‑Net’s ratio loss is introduced to prevent the model from collapsing to trivial solutions such as keeping almost all vectors (which would remove computational savings) or compressing too aggressively and discarding essential information [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, arXiv:2507.07955v2, p. 8, Section 2.2.3 Ratio Loss]. The loss provides continuous feedback via the average boundary probability G to steer the fraction of selected vectors F toward a target compression ratio [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, arXiv:2507.07955v2, p. 8, Section 2.2.3 Ratio Loss][Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, arXiv:2507.07955v2, p. 8, Section 2.2.3 Ratio Loss]. In the combined training objective the ratio loss is weighted by a hyper‑parameter α, which the authors fix to 0.03 in all experiments [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, arXiv:2507.07955v2, p. 8, Section 2.2.3 Ratio Loss].
answer_raw: H‑Net’s ratio loss is introduced to prevent the model from collapsing to trivial solutions such as keeping almost all vectors (which would remove computational savings) or compressing too aggressively and discarding essential information [P3]. The loss provides continuous feedback via the average boundary probability G to steer the fraction of selected vectors F toward a target compression ratio [P3][P1]. In the combined training objective the ratio loss is weighted by a hyper‑parameter α, which the authors fix to 0.03 in all experiments [P1].

question: What happened in the H-Net ablation when the smoothing module was removed?
answer: When the smoothing module was removed, training became unstable: compression‑ratio values fluctuated wildly and the model could not learn consistent chunking boundaries, leading to a substantial degradation in validation bits‑per‑byte performance. question: How is positional information encoded in the original Transformer compared with Moshi's Helium language model?
answer: The original Transformer adds sinusoidal positional encodings, computed with sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, to the token embeddings so that each dimension follows a fixed sinusoid and the wavelengths form a geometric progression [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 6, Section 3.5 Positional Encoding]. Moshi’s Helium model replaces those sinusoidal encodings with rotary positional embeddings (RoPE), which incorporate position information directly into the attention mechanism via rotation of query and key vectors [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 7, Section 3.2.1 Architecture].
answer_raw:
The original Transformer adds sinusoidal positional encodings, computed with sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, to the token embeddings so that each dimension follows a fixed sinusoid and the wavelengths form a geometric progression [P1].  
Moshi’s Helium model replaces those sinusoidal encodings with rotary positional embeddings (RoPE), which incorporate position information directly into the attention mechanism via rotation of query and key vectors [P3].
citations: [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 6, Section 3.5 Positional Encoding]
[Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 7, Section 3.2.1 Architecture]

question: Moshi and H-Net both describe hierarchical models. What does each level of the hierarchy operate over in each paper?
answer: Moshi’s hierarchy consists of a Temporal Transformer that processes the most recent low‑level representation Vs‑1 (the sum of K learned embedding tables) and a Depth Transformer that processes higher‑level latent variables zs together with an embedding of the preceding higher‑level state Vs,k‑1 [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 14, Section 3.4.1 Hierarchical autoregressive modeling with RQ-Transformer]. H‑Net’s hierarchy first processes the raw input signal with a small encoder, then operates on recursively compressed chunks in a main network, and finally upsamples and decodes back to the original‑resolution data [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, arXiv:2507.07955v2, p. 2, Section 1 Introduction].
answer_raw:
Moshi’s hierarchy consists of a Temporal Transformer that processes the most recent low‑level representation Vs‑1 (the sum of K learned embedding tables) and a Depth Transformer that processes higher‑level latent variables zs together with an embedding of the preceding higher‑level state Vs,k‑1 [P2].  
H‑Net’s hierarchy first processes the raw input signal with a small encoder, then operates on recursively compressed chunks in a main network, and finally upsamples and decodes back to the original‑resolution data [P4].

question: What input units does each of the three models consume: the Transformer for translation, Moshi, and H-Net?
answer: The Transformer used for machine‑translation receives a sequence of text tokens as its input, whose length determines the maximum output length during inference [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 8, Section 6.1 Machine Translation]. Moshi jointly consumes two parallel token streams: a text stream Wₖ and an audio stream Aₛ,ₖ (semantic + acoustic tokens) for each timestep k [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 58, Section Appendix D. Characterizing Audio Artifacts Caused by Quantization]. H‑Net first processes raw byte sequences, drawing boundaries at spacelike bytes (and at the start of each word in its first stage) and then groups these bytes into higher‑level units such as whole words or numbering tokens in its second stage [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, arXiv:2507.07955v2, p. 15, Section 3.1 Language Modeling][Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, arXiv:2507.07955v2, p. 15, Section 3.1 Language Modeling].
answer_raw:
The Transformer used for machine‑translation receives a sequence of text tokens as its input, whose length determines the maximum output length during inference [P1].  
Moshi jointly consumes two parallel token streams: a text stream Wₖ and an audio stream Aₛ,ₖ (semantic + acoustic tokens) for each timestep k [P3].  
H‑Net first processes raw byte sequences, drawing boundaries at spacelike bytes (and at the start of each word in its first stage) and then groups these bytes into higher‑level units such as whole words or numbering tokens in its second stage [P5][P6].
